problem_motivation.content: A recurring methodological gap in passive-film/PDM corrosion modeling is that mechanistic models with many parameters are routinely fit to sparse measurements and extrapolated over long time horizons without formally testing identifiability; with only three exposure times (six layer means) for a five-parameter reduced model—and even more rates before reduction—a good fit does not show which parameters are actually constrained, yet that determines whether extrapolations can be trusted.
evidence_spans: Mechanistic corrosion models are routinely fitted with four to six parameters to a few measurements and extrapolated across service lifetimes, yet whether the data determine them is rarely tested.
The question this paper is built around is a methodological gap that recurs across four decades of PDM parameter estimation.
Written this way the two layers are still independent, and the six rates in Eqs. (5) and (7) are far more than three exposure times can determine.

Six layer means at three exposure times against a five-parameter model is the ratio that dictates both the objective below and the identifiability machinery carried alongside it: at this sample size a good fit is not evidence that the parameters are determined, and the two questions have to be asked separately.
We then ask the question that decides what the identification is worth, namely which parameters the three exposure times actually determine

If three chromium points carry the fit, the question that decides what the fit is worth is which of the five parameters those points actually determine, and the answer governs every extrapolation in Section 3.3, since a parameter the data do not constrain cannot be relied on outside the window that failed to constrain it)
The correct statement is therefore not that the identification disagrees with stoichiometry, but that three exposure times cannot separate oxide production from oxide loss.
